Located along the scenic American River Parkway and operated by Sacramento County Regional Parks, Sailor Bar offers miles of trails winding through oak woodlands, meadows, and river bluffs. It remains a favorite destination for hikers, wildlife watchers, and families seeking a peaceful escape into both nature and history.
 
The Friends of Sailor Bar (FOSB) works in close partnership with Sacramento Regional Parks to preserve and enhance the park’s natural beauty, wildlife habitat, and historical resources.
 
To enhance visitor experience and accessibility, through the generous donations of our community, FOSB recently acquired seventeen new benches and tables which have been installed throughout the park. We have also launched monthly interpretive programs designed to educate and inspire park visitors.
 
A previous plan to allow motor vehicles deeper into Sailor Bar has been abandoned. Our collective focus has successfully shifted to education, habitat restoration, and ensuring Sailor Bar is utilized in a way that benefits both human visitors and the wildlife that call it home.
 
FOSB extends its sincere thanks to those who make our work possible:
• District 3 Supervisor Rich Desmond & Liz Bellas (Director of Regional Parks), for their continuous guidance and unwavering support of Sailor Bar.
• The Sacramento Regional Parks Maintenance Staff, whose daily hard work keeps the park clean, safe, and beautiful for everyone.

contentHtml:
The Friends of Sailor Bar (FOSB) are dedicated to cultivating a community who values and actively supports the wildlife and their habitat along the American River, beginning with Sailor Bar. We also believe that the history of Sailor Bar and the American River can inform us on how human actions over time can change nature.   Finally, we are committed to providing opportunities for people with disabilities to enjoy nature and the history of Sailor Bar.

We are a grassroots modern-day community of compassionate nature-loving people who have fun working together to create opportunities to bring people to nature, and nature to people.

The hub of the FOSB consists of 10 talented volunteers who serve as the FOSB Stellar Steering Committee. The FOSB SSC works together to ensure that we are aligned and actively serving our mission and priorities. Everyone on the FOSB SSC is compassionate “doers”, reliable and dedicated.

Our values are to do our best to show Love and Grace, have fun, be nimble and to continually learn and evolve.

Our Compassion in Action priorities are:

· Keep Sailor Bar safe, pristine and a haven for people and animals to enjoy the quiet of Nature while ensuring that the well-being of wildlife is of the utmost priority.

· Host volunteer meetups to remove invasive plants that are harmful to the biodiversity of Sailor Bar, and sow native seeds and sprouts to enhance biodiversity.

· Provide opportunities for people with disabilities to enjoy being at Sailor Bar by partnering with the Sacramento County Disability Advisory Commission, Regional Parks, California Native Plant Society and the disabled and non-disabled community in our endeavor to create a native plant sensory butterfly and bird garden with an adjoining All Persons Trail at Turtle Pond.

· Host monthly Fun and Educational Exciting events at Sailor Bar that emphasizes the importance of respecting the only Federally and State designated Wild and Scenic River running through an urban environment that we have right here in our community. The River is our Life Force!

· Utilize the rich history of Sailor Bar to teach share the heritage of the original indigenous inhabitants and the pioneers who came here during and after the gold rush. (This history chronicles the environmental impacts that gold mining, dredging and dams can have on a river system and about how, over time, nature can heal itself and recover into a rich riparian habitat for a variety of wildlife.)

· Establish and maintain partnerships with organizations and community leaders who are dedicated to maintaining, upholding and nurturing wildlife habitats.

HOW TO ENTER SAILOR BAR

     Enter from Olive Avenue in Fair Oaks – 8266 Olive Avenue

     Enter from Illinois Avenue in Fair Oaks- 4253 Illinois Avenue

 

Sailor Bar is located along the shore of the American River Parkway.

Our sites are operated as part of Sacramento Regional County Parks. You will enjoy discovering the miles of trails as they wind through Oak Woodlands, meadows, a large pond and river bluffs. We are a favorite destination for hikers, wildlife watchers and families seeking a peaceful escape.

Sailor Bar is a Haven for Wildlife

Sailor Bar supports an impressive diversity of wildlife and native plants. Visitors frequently encounter mule deer, coyotes, foxes, skunks, wild turkeys, river otters, beavers, turtles and many reptiles.

Bird watchers will find exceptional opportunities – with more than 200 species recorded! Species include waterbirds, Bald Eagles, hawks, woodpeckers, songbirds and seasonally migrating wildlife. You will also find several Great Blue Heron rookeries (nests) located at Sailor Bar.

contentHtml:
Sailor Bar is a park with a lot of history and wonderful present day opportunities. Settled by gold-seeking sailors, this park was dredged for gold during the Gold Rush. Today, visitor activities such as rafting, fishing, horseback riding and nature gazing, have replaced the adventures of historic explorers. 

How to Get There

From U.S. 50, exit onto Hazel Avenue. Make a left at Winding Way, then another left on Illinois Avenue. The park entrance will be at the bottom of a small hill.

​​​Activities

  • Sailor Bar is a very popular launching spot for small watercraft and rafts. A gravel road provides launch access.
  • An equestrian trail weaves through the park, while access to the Jedediah Smith Memorial Bike Trail can be found across the river.
  • Early fall finds fishing enthusiasts’ eager to take advantage of both pond and river fishing. A fishing pond near the river offers year-round angling.
  • Also near this pond is a nature trail that leads to riparian (riverside) and historic locations where deer, coyotes, hawks and owls may be seen.

Hours and Fees

The park is open year-round from sunrise to sunset. Parking fees are collected year-round, even on special event days and on weekends.

Park Fees

  • $8 Vehicle
  • $15 Vehicles with Trailer (ex. Boat or Horse) or RV​
  • $30 Bus
  • Vehicle fees increase over Summer Holiday Weekends.​

Special Event fees vary by event.
Self-payment is required if no fee collector is present.

Picnics Allowed: Yes​

title: Birding at Sailor Bar
excerpt: Discover 218 Species of Birds Along the American River If you love birds—or have ever wanted to learn more about them— Sailor Bar on the American River is a wonderful place to…
contentHtml:
Discover 218 Species of Birds Along the American River

If you love birds—or have ever wanted to learn more about them—Sailor Bar on the American River is a wonderful place to begin.

Located along the American River Parkway in Fair Oaks, Sailor Bar offers an extraordinary variety of habitats within a relatively compact area. The river, riparian forests, oak woodlands, ponds, gravel bars, open areas and mature trees provide food, shelter and nesting habitat for an impressive variety of birds.

In fact, at least 218 species of birds have been recorded at Sailor Bar. Sacramento County’s Sailor Bar All Persons Trail Vision Plan identifies the area as the #2 eBird hotspot along the lower American River, with 218 species recorded—just three species behind William B. Pond at the time of the plan’s publication.

A Different Birding Experience Around Every Bend

One of the things that makes Sailor Bar so special for birdwatching is the diversity of its landscape.

Along the river, keep an eye out for birds that depend on the riparian environment. Willow, alder, cottonwood and other riverside vegetation provide habitat for a wide variety of songbirds and other wildlife. In the oak woodland and more open areas, you may encounter hawks, woodpeckers, finches, sparrows and many other species.

The pond and surrounding vegetation provide another opportunity to discover birds. Depending on the season, birders may encounter Pied-billed Grebes, Mallards, Red-winged Blackbirds, Red-shouldered Hawks, Hutton’s Vireos, Fox Sparrows, Hermit Thrushes and Lincoln’s Sparrows, among many others.

And don’t forget to look up. Raptors, herons and other large birds can make a spectacular appearance overhead or in the trees.

Birding Through the Seasons

There is no single “best” time to go birding at Sailor Bar because the bird community changes throughout the year.

Spring brings returning migrants and the activity of nesting birds. Summer offers opportunities to observe resident species as well as birds raising their young. Fall migration can bring new species through the area, while winter offers its own rewards, including seasonal visitors and birds that are easier to spot among the more open vegetation.

That means every visit to Sailor Bar can be different.

A walk you take in January may reveal an entirely different collection of birds than the same walk in May or October.

You Don’t Have to Be an Expert Birder

One of the great things about birding at Sailor Bar is that you don’t have to know the names of the birds before you arrive.

Bring a pair of binoculars if you have them, slow down, and listen.

And bring your smartphone!

Let Merlin Help You Identify What You Find

If you’re new to birdwatching, one of the best companions you can have in the field is Merlin Bird ID, the free bird-identification app from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology.

Merlin can help identify a bird in several ways. You can answer simple questions about what you see, take a photograph, or—one of the most exciting features—use Sound ID to listen to the birds singing around you. Merlin provides real-time suggestions of birds it thinks you may be hearing.

Merlin is particularly useful at Sailor Bar because sometimes you hear a bird before you ever see it.

That mysterious song coming from somewhere in the trees? Let Merlin listen.

The bird that disappeared before you could get a good look? Take a photograph and let Merlin suggest possibilities.

The unfamiliar bird sitting across the river? Use Merlin’s identification tools to help narrow down what you are seeing.

Merlin is not a substitute for learning to identify birds yourself—and it isn’t always right. The Cornell Lab recommends treating its suggestions as a starting point and comparing the bird, photograph or recording with the information provided by the app.

That’s actually part of the fun.

Use Merlin as your birding coach. Over time, you’ll begin recognizing the songs, calls, shapes, colors and behaviors on your own.

Explore Sailor Bar’s 218 Recorded Species

For birders who want to go beyond a casual walk, the Sailor Bar eBird hotspot is an invaluable resource.

eBird is a worldwide citizen-science project where birdwatchers record their observations. The Sailor Bar hotspot provides a comprehensive record of the birds that have been documented at the site.

With 218 species recorded, the list gives you an excellent idea of just how rich Sailor Bar’s birdlife can be—and it can turn your next visit into a birding adventure.

Before heading out, take a look at the Sailor Bar species list and pick a few birds you’d especially like to find. Then bring your binoculars, open Merlin, and start exploring.

Explore the Sailor Bar eBird species list

More Than Just Birdwatching

Birding at Sailor Bar is about more than checking species off a list.

It is about standing quietly beside the American River and hearing the calls of birds in the trees. It is watching a Great Blue Heron move along the shoreline. It is spotting a hawk circling overhead or a songbird moving through the willows. It is discovering that the “little brown bird” you’ve walked past a hundred times has a name—and a fascinating story.

And because Sailor Bar is part of the American River Parkway, birding is just one part of a much larger natural experience.

Here, the river, trees, wildlife and changing seasons come together to create a place where there is always something new to see, hear and learn.

Come Discover the Birds of Sailor Bar

Whether you are an experienced birder with a life list, a photographer looking for your next subject, a family introducing children to nature, or someone who simply enjoys walking along the river, Sailor Bar is a remarkable place to discover the birds of the American River.

Bring your binoculars.

Bring your curiosity.

Download Merlin.

And give yourself time to stop, look and listen.

You may be surprised by how many birds are waiting to be discovered at Sailor Bar.

A great place to start:
Explore the Sailor Bar eBird hotspot before your visit and see how many of its 218 recorded species you can find.

title: Plant Life
excerpt: The diverse plant life documented on the Sailor Bar Biodiversity Project on iNaturalist spans several distinct ecological zones, from moist riverbanks to dry upland gravel…
contentHtml:
The diverse plant life documented on the Sailor Bar Biodiversity Project on iNaturalist spans several distinct ecological zones, from moist riverbanks to dry upland gravel tailings. 
 
Here are the key plant species you can find across these habitats:
 

Riparian Trees and Canopy

    • Fremont Cottonwood (Populus fremontii): The largest fast-growing tree dominating the river’s edge, creating crucial shade and structural canopy for the ecosystem. 
    • Willows (Salix spp.): Plentiful along the floodplains and shoreline, these trees help stabilize the banks against erosion and thrive in moist soils. 
    • White Alder (Alnus rhombifolia): Stands of alder line the waterways, contributing to the dense, shaded riparian corridors that cool the riverbanks. 

Oak Woodland Staples

    • Valley Oak (Quercus lobata) & Blue Oak (Quercus douglasii): Found slightly further back from the water where the soil improves, these long-lived oaks anchor the park’s woodlands. 
    • Coyote Brush (Baccharis pilularis): A resilient, evergreen native shrub that dominates the transitions between the woodlands and open grasslands.  
    • Blue Elderberry (Sambucus cerulea):  A large, deciduous shrub that can grow to 6 metres (20 ft) in height and width.

Wildflowers and Ground Cover

    • Mountain Garland (Clarkia unguiculata): A beautiful native wildflower that paints the open fields and dirt paths with pink and purple blooms during the late spring. [1]
    • Yerba Mansa (Anemopsis californica): A native perennial found in the damp seeps and pond edges, recognized by its distinct cone-shaped white flowers that turn red in the fall. 

Invasive Species of Concern

 
  • Yellow Star-Thistle (Centaurea solstitialis): A highly aggressive, non-native weed that blankets the dry gravel tailings, outcompeting native grasses. 
  • Red Water Fern (Azolla filiculoides): An opportunistic species that occasionally forms thick, carpet-like layers over stagnant waters, such as the park’s Turtle Pond.

title: Salmon and Steelhead Runs at Sailor Bar
excerpt: Each fall, Chinook salmon return from the Pacific Ocean to the American River to spawn, typically from September through November. Steelhead trout make a similar journey during…
contentHtml:
Each fall, Chinook salmon return from the Pacific Ocean to the American River to spawn, typically from September through November.  Steelhead trout make a similar journey during winter months.   Sailor Bar is one of the best locations on the river to watch the Chinook and Steelhead runs.

Historic Runs

 

The American River once supported massive runs of Chinook salmon. Fish traveled from the Pacific Ocean to spawn in upstream gravel beds.

Spawning Process

Female salmon create shallow nests in the gravel called redds, where they deposit their eggs.  Walking on or near redds can destroy an entire generation of fish.  Please avoid these areas and help protect this remarkable natural cycle.

Completion of Folsom Dam in 1955

Built in the 1950s for flood control, water storage, and hydropower, the completion of Folsom Dam had a substantial impact on the lower American River and on the Chinook Salmon and Steelhead Trout runs.

The Completion of Folsom Dam Dramatically Changed the River and Salmon/Steelhead Runs

  • Folsom dam reduced natural flooding and stabilized river flows but blocked access to historic upstream spawning grounds so the Salmon and Steelhead can only spawn in lower sections of the River (like at Sailor Bar)
  • The dam trapped sediment (sand and gravel) upstream that historically replenished the gravel beds used by the Salmon and Steelhead to spawn
  • The Nimbus Fish Hatchery (just up river from Sailor Bar) was built to help mitigate the loss of spawning habitat
  • Periodically the Water Forum must now conduct periodic restoration projects to replenish the gravel spawning beds at locations like Sailor Bar as water releases from the dam continue to erode the gravel beds that remain in the Lower American river
  • Fewer large floods  on the lower American River meant less natural reshaping of the river
  • Cooler, regulated flows as a result of the dam change ecological patterns
  • Loss of some natural floodplain processes

Today, the American River is a place of recovery, resilience, and renewed stewardship — where communities are working to protect and restore the ecological and cultural richness that once defined this landscape.

title: The Elderberry: An Ancient Plant with an Important Story
excerpt: Along the American River at Sailor Bar, among the willows, oaks and other native plants, grow shrubs that can easily be overlooked. They are blue elderberries —plants with a…
contentHtml:
Along the American River at Sailor Bar, among the willows, oaks and other native plants, grow shrubs that can easily be overlooked. They are blue elderberries—plants with a remarkable connection to the people, wildlife and natural history of the American River.

For generations, Native people of the Sacramento Valley recognized elderberry as a plant with many gifts. Today, the same shrubs provide food and shelter for wildlife and serve as the only known host plant for the Valley Elderberry Longhorn Beetle, a federally threatened species found only in California’s Central Valley.

The elderberry is much more than a shrub. It is part of the living history of Sailor Bar.

A Plant Important to the First People of the American River

Long before Sailor Bar became a place for gold miners, dredges, hikers and fishermen, the American River was home to Native people whose lives were intimately connected to the plants and animals of the river valley.

The Sacramento Valley was—and remains—the homeland of the Nisenan and other Native peoples. Their knowledge of the landscape included an understanding of when plants should be harvested, how they could be used, and how people could live within the natural cycles of the land.

Elderberry was one of those important plants.

The Nisenan name for elderberry is nok. Traditional knowledge recorded among the Nisenan and neighboring Maidu communities describes many uses for elderberry. Its berries could be gathered and preserved, while its straight, relatively soft branches could be fashioned into useful objects and musical instruments.

Across California, Indigenous peoples used elderberry for food, medicine, dyes and tools. The flowers and other portions of the plant had medicinal uses, while the hollow stems were particularly useful for making musical instruments.

This relationship with elderberry was not simply one of taking resources from the landscape. Traditional ecological knowledge emphasized timing, care and balance. Native people actively managed many plant communities, using practices such as carefully timed burning to maintain productive landscapes.

And this relationship has not disappeared.

Native people are still here. Contemporary Nisenan, Maidu and other California Native communities continue to maintain cultural connections with elderberry and the landscapes in which it grows. As one Native ethnobotanist has expressed, elderberry is part of an ecological relationship involving the plant, the insect and people—not simply a resource for one of them.

A Feast for Wildlife

Elderberry is also an important part of the American River’s riparian ecosystem.

Its flowers provide nectar for insects and other pollinators. Later in the year, its clusters of berries become food for birds and other animals. Elderberry shrubs also provide cover, nesting habitat and perches.

Blue elderberry is used by a wide variety of wildlife, including numerous species of birds and mammals.

That makes the elderberry especially valuable at Sailor Bar, where riparian vegetation, oak woodland, meadow and river habitats occur together.

The Friends of Sailor Bar has documented the remarkable wildlife diversity of the park, including more than 200 species of birds as well as mammals such as deer, foxes, coyotes, beavers and river otters.

The elderberry is one small but important piece of this larger web of life.

And Then There Is the Beetle

Perhaps the most surprising creature associated with Sailor Bar’s elderberries is one that most visitors will never see.

Meet the Valley Elderberry Longhorn Beetle
Desmocerus californicus dimorphus

 
 
 
6

This colorful beetle is found only in California’s Central Valley and depends on elderberry for essentially its entire life cycle.

That makes the relationship extraordinarily specialized:

No elderberry → no elderberry beetle.

The beetle spends most of its life hidden inside the stems of elderberry shrubs.

Adult beetles lay their eggs on elderberry foliage. The tiny larvae then bore into the stems, where they feed and develop within the soft inner pith. Eventually, after completing their transformation, adult beetles chew their way out of the stems.

The small round openings that appear in older elderberry stems can therefore tell an important story.

They may be evidence that a beetle has completed its development and emerged from the shrub.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service notes that many records of the beetle are based on these exit holes, because the beetle itself spends so much of its life concealed inside elderberry stems.

Look—but don’t disturb

If you see holes in an elderberry stem, don’t poke a stick into them or break open the branch to see what’s inside.

The stem may be home to a beetle.

A seemingly ordinary elderberry bush can contain an entire hidden world.

Why Did the Beetle Become Threatened?

The story of the elderberry beetle is also a story about what happened to California’s rivers.

The Central Valley once contained enormous expanses of riparian forest. Over time, much of this habitat was cleared, altered or fragmented.

When the Valley Elderberry Longhorn Beetle was listed as threatened under the federal Endangered Species Act in 1980, it was known from only a handful of locations. One of those early locations was the American River in Sacramento County.

Today, the beetle is known from considerably more locations, but its dependence on elderberry remains.

And that is why protecting elderberry shrubs matters.

The American River Parkway Natural Resources Management Plan specifically recognizes elderberry habitat as important for the beetle, and elderberry restoration has occurred at several locations along the Parkway, including Sailor Bar.

A Shrub That Connects Past and Future

Standing beside an elderberry at Sailor Bar, it is easy to see only a shrub.

But look a little closer.

Its berries connect us to the people who lived along the American River for thousands of years.

Its flowers and fruit connect it to birds, insects and other wildlife.

Its stems may shelter a beetle that spends almost its entire life hidden from view.

And its presence connects today’s American River Parkway with the native riparian forests that once covered much more of the Central Valley.

One plant. Three stories.

Culture. Wildlife. Conservation.

That is why the elderberry deserves our attention.

Help Protect Sailor Bar’s Elderberries

When visiting Sailor Bar:

  • Stay on established trails where possible.
  • Do not cut, break or collect elderberry branches.
  • Do not disturb holes in elderberry stems. They may be evidence of the Valley Elderberry Longhorn Beetle.
  • Leave berries, flowers and branches for the wildlife and insects that depend on them.
  • Take photographs rather than specimens.
  • Help others understand why these seemingly ordinary shrubs are important.

The best way to experience Sailor Bar is to leave its natural communities intact for the next visitor—and for the wildlife and plants that call the American River home.

A final thought

The next time you walk past an elderberry at Sailor Bar, stop for a moment.

Look at the flowers. Look at the berries. Look closely at the stems.

You may be standing beside a plant that has provided food and useful materials to Native people for generations—and that may, right now, be sheltering a beetle that exists nowhere else on Earth.

At Sailor Bar, even an ordinary-looking shrub can have an extraordinary story.

contentHtml:
Discover the Vibrant Wildlife of Sailor Bar
 
Nestled along the rugged banks of the American River in Fair Oaks, California, Sailor Bar Park is a premier natural haven for a diverse mix of native California wildlife. Its unique blend of rushing river currents, calm pond waters, open gravel bars, and dense oak woodlands creates a thriving ecosystem where visitors can experience nature up close.
🦅 A Birdwatcher’s Paradise
With more than 200 recorded species, Sailor Bar is a vital stop on the Pacific Flyway and a dream destination for birders.
  • Apex Raptors: Look up to see Bald Eagles, Red-tailed Hawks, and Osprey hunting above the river.
  • River & Pond Waders: Spot Great Blue Herons, Great Egrets, and American White Pelicans feeding along the shoreline.
  • Woodland Residents: Listen for the distinct calls of Wild Turkeys, California Quail, and Acorn Woodpeckers.
  • Seasonal Migrants: Welcome colorful Bullock’s Orioles in the spring and Fox Sparrows in the winter.

🦊 Mammals of the Oak Woodlands & Riverbanks
The park’s preserved corridors offer safe habitats for a variety of land and semi-aquatic mammals.
  • Mule Deer: Often seen quietly browsing near the nature trails during the peaceful early morning hours.
  • River Otters & Beavers: Watch the water’s edge to catch these playful, highly active aquatic mammals swimming.
  • Native Predators: Coyotes and gray foxes occasionally travel the rugged mine tailings and brush lines.

🐍 Aquatic Life & Reptiles
The unique pairing of the swift American River and the calm, historic Sailor Bar fishing pond supports a rich underwater and reptilian community.
  • Migratory Salmon: The river serves as a critical spawning ground for Chinook salmon and steelhead trout.
  • Pond Fish: The neighboring still waters host largemouth bass, bluegill, and black crappie.
  • Sun-Seeking Reptiles: Look closely at fallen logs to spot Western Pond Turtles and California whiptail lizards soaking up the sun.
  • Native Snakes: Northern Pacific Rattlesnakes live in the park and can be found basking on rocks, logs, or trails during the warmer months.

⚠️ Important Rattlesnake Safety: Rattlesnakes are an important part of the ecosystem but should always be avoided. Stay on designated trails, keep pets on a leash, look carefully before stepping over logs or rocks, and never approach or attempt to handle a snake. If you hear a rattle, freeze, locate the snake, and slowly step back to give it plenty of space.

title: A Detailed History of Sailor Bar
excerpt: Sailor Bar, on the American River in Fair Oaks, is a landscape where several chapters of Sacramento County history can still be seen today. Long before gold miners arrived, the…
contentHtml:
Sailor Bar, on the American River in Fair Oaks, is a landscape where several chapters of Sacramento County history can still be seen today. Long before gold miners arrived, the American River was home to Nisenan people. During the Gold Rush, Sailor Bar became a center of placer mining. Later, powerful hydraulic mining equipment and enormous bucket-line dredges radically reshaped the land. Today, the rocky tailings, steep bluffs, river channel, and surviving native vegetation provide visible reminders of that history.

Before the Gold Rush: The Nisenan

For thousands of years, the lower American River was part of the homeland of the Nisenan, also known as the Southern Maidu. Nisenan communities occupied the lower American River and surrounding Sacramento Valley, taking advantage of the river’s abundant plants, fish, wildlife, and other resources. Archaeological and ethnographic evidence documents Nisenan villages and resource use throughout this portion of the American River watershed.

At Sailor Bar, visitors can still find exposed bedrock and hardpan surfaces containing grinding features. Local historical accounts identify these as places where Indigenous people probably processed acorns and other foods. These features are particularly significant because much of the surrounding landscape was later disturbed by mining.

The river itself was an important source of food and transportation. Salmon and other fish, waterfowl, plants, and game were among the resources available to Nisenan communities living along the American River.

From Nisenan Homeland to Private Land

Before the Gold Rush, the land around Sailor Bar was part of the traditional homeland of the Nisenan people. European and American concepts of private land ownership did not govern the Nisenan use of the American River and its surrounding resources.

During the Mexican period of California history (1821–1846), the Mexican government began granting large tracts of land to individuals. These Mexican land grants became the foundation for many of the private property boundaries that developed in the Sacramento region.

Sailor Bar lies within the general area of Rancho San Juan, a Mexican land grant of approximately 20,000 acres. In 1844, Mexican Governor Manuel Micheltorena granted Rancho San Juan to Joel P. Dedmond. The grant extended along the American River and included portions of what are now Fair Oaks, Orangevale, and Carmichael.

Dedmond subsequently sold his interest in the rancho to Hiram Grimes. Following the Mexican-American War, the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo required the United States to honor legitimate Mexican land grants. Under the federal Land Act of 1851, landowners were required to present their claims to the newly established U.S. Board of Land Commissioners. The Rancho San Juan claim was filed in 1852, and the grant was ultimately patented to Hiram Grimes in 1860.

This transition was significant. Within only a few years, the legal framework governing the American River landscape had changed from Indigenous occupation and use, to Mexican land grants, and then to American private property recognized through the federal land-claim process.

The Gold Rush soon complicated this developing system of ownership. Thousands of miners and settlers arrived in the Sacramento region, often occupying or mining land without regard to existing claims. Mining activity along the American River also created a new distinction between ownership of the land and the right to extract valuable minerals from it. In practice, the rush for gold frequently overwhelmed existing property boundaries and led to disputes over who had the right to occupy, mine, or profit from particular areas.

Sailor Bar’s subsequent history reflects these changing concepts of land use. What had first been a Nisenan landscape became part of a Mexican land grant, then private property, and eventually a public park within the American River Parkway.

The Gold Rush Comes to Sailor Bar

The discovery of gold at Sutter’s Mill in 1848 transformed the American River almost overnight. Gold was discovered at Sailor Bar around 1850, and miners soon worked the rich placer deposits found in the river gravels. By the middle of the 1850s, much of the easily recovered gold in the American River’s valley deposits had already been taken, but mining at Sailor Bar continued using increasingly sophisticated methods.

The origin of the name Sailor Bar is part history and part legend. According to the long-standing local story, a sailor—or sailors—jumped ship during the Gold Rush and came ashore to search for gold. Sacramento County Regional Parks describes this as a local legend rather than a documented fact.

Early miners worked the gravel with relatively simple equipment: gold pans, rockers, sluice boxes, and other tools used to separate gold from river gravel. Later miners returned to ground that had already been worked, searching for gold that earlier miners had missed. Chinese miners were among those who participated in this continuing placer-mining activity throughout the region.

Hydraulic Mining Reshapes the Landscape

As the easily accessible gold was removed, miners turned to more powerful methods. Hydraulic mining used high-pressure streams of water to wash away hillsides and expose gold-bearing gravel.

The steep bluffs at Sailor Bar contain evidence of this period. Water was directed against the gravel deposits, washing sediment downhill while miners recovered the heavier gold. The process was enormously destructive to the landscape. Local historical accounts identify the bluffs and other altered terrain at Sailor Bar as remnants of hydraulic mining.

Hydraulic mining also demonstrated a fundamental problem with gold extraction along the American River: recovering the remaining gold required moving enormous quantities of earth and rock.

The Age of the Gold Dredge

By the late nineteenth century, mining technology had changed again. Instead of miners working the river gravel by hand, large floating dredges could excavate enormous quantities of material and process it mechanically.

Sailor Bar became part of this new industrial era. In 1899, the Ashburton Mining Company drilled test holes at Sailor Bar to determine whether the gravel was rich enough to justify constructing a dredge. The tests proved promising, and construction of a large dredge began. A local historical account published in the early twentieth century describes the dredge as the Hercules, which was launched in 1900 and subsequently equipped for large-scale operations.

The Hercules was essentially a floating mining factory. A continuous chain of large buckets scooped gravel from the riverbed and carried it aboard the dredge. There, the material was washed and sorted. Gold was recovered from the finer material while larger rocks were discarded behind the dredge.

The scale of the operation was remarkable. Contemporary descriptions report that the dredge used a bucket line of 63 buckets, each weighing approximately 1,800 pounds after modifications. The dredge could excavate a swath roughly 200 feet wide, processing tens of thousands of cubic feet of material during a day’s operation.

The result can still be seen throughout Sailor Bar.

The Tailings

The long, irregular ridges of rounded rocks that cover much of Sailor Bar are dredge tailings—the material left behind after miners removed and processed the river gravel in search of gold.

The tailings are more than piles of rocks. They are a physical record of the industrial mining process. The dredges excavated the river and surrounding deposits, processed the material, and deposited the waste rock in long rows behind them. Sacramento County’s Natural Resources Management Plan notes that dredger mining substantially altered the majority of the Sailor Bar landscape, removing vegetation and leaving large piles of cobble material that remain prominent today.

Walking through Sailor Bar today, visitors are therefore walking across a landscape largely created by the machinery of the gold-mining era.

From Mining Landscape to Natural Area

Mining did not end the story of Sailor Bar. After decades of mining and other industrial activity, the disturbed landscape gradually began to recover.

Some areas remain dominated by barren or sparsely vegetated tailings, while other depressions and areas that escaped intensive disturbance developed into pockets of oak woodland, riparian vegetation, and wetlands. Sacramento County’s current management plan recognizes these “pocket forests” as important habitat within an otherwise heavily altered landscape.

This combination of natural recovery and historic disturbance is one of the things that makes Sailor Bar unusual. The landscape simultaneously preserves evidence of nineteenth- and twentieth-century mining while supporting plants and wildlife that have adapted to the altered terrain.

Sailor Bar Becomes Part of the Parkway

Sailor Bar entered a new chapter in the twentieth century as the community began to acquire and preserve land along the American River.

In 1964, the Fair Oaks Recreation and Park District purchased approximately 85 acres at Sailor Bar from Russell Gallaway Jr. for $85,000. At the time, it was the largest park-site purchase in the district’s history. Two years later, the district developed plans for a $120,000 park improvement project, including an ambitious proposal for a man-made lake. The lake project ultimately failed, and the planned lake was never completed.

In 1972, the park district traded the Sailor Bar property to Sacramento County in exchange for a 30-acre site near Phoenix Field. The transfer brought Sailor Bar into the American River Parkway system, where it became part of a larger effort to protect the American River corridor for recreation, wildlife, and future generations.

A River Changed by Dams

Sailor Bar’s history did not end when mining declined. The construction of Folsom and Nimbus dams fundamentally changed the American River’s flow and sediment system.

Nimbus Dam, completed in 1955, blocks salmon from reaching their historic spawning areas farther upstream. The dams also interrupt the natural movement of gravel downstream. As a result, the lower American River has become relatively starved of the gravel that salmon need to create spawning beds.

This created an unexpected connection between Sailor Bar’s mining history and its modern ecological role. The same river gravels that attracted gold miners in the nineteenth century are essential to salmon today.

Restoring the River

Beginning in the twenty-first century, Sailor Bar became an important site for salmon and steelhead habitat restoration.

Restoration projects have placed carefully selected gravel into the American River near Sailor Bar to recreate suitable spawning habitat. In 2022, for example, the Bureau of Reclamation and the Water Forum worked together on a major gravel-placement project, adding tons of gravel to the river and shaping it into habitat where Chinook salmon and steelhead could spawn.

The effort illustrates how dramatically the river’s history has come full circle. The river that once attracted miners because of its gold-bearing gravel is now being restored in part because those same gravels are essential to the survival of native salmon.

Sailor Bar Today

Today, Sailor Bar is part of the American River Parkway and is managed by Sacramento County Regional Parks. Visitors come to hike, fish, ride horses, launch small boats and rafts, observe wildlife, and enjoy the river.

But beneath the recreational landscape is a remarkable historical record.

The grinding rocks along the riverbank tell of the Nisenan people who lived here long before the Gold Rush. The bluffs bear evidence of hydraulic mining. The enormous piles of rounded cobbles record the work of the dredges. And the restored gravel beds in the river reflect today’s effort to repair some of the ecological damage caused by more than a century of human alteration.

Sailor Bar is therefore much more than a beautiful place along the American River. It is a landscape shaped by Indigenous history, the Gold Rush, industrial mining, community conservation, and modern ecological restoration—all visible within a relatively small area.

Sources

  • Sacramento County Regional Parks, Sailor Bar and American River Parkway information.
  • Sacramento County Regional Parks, American River Parkway Natural Resources Management Plan, Sailor Bar Area Plan.
  • Fair Oaks Historical Society, History of the Fair Oaks Recreation and Park District.
  • Fair Oaks High School historical archive, early twentieth-century account of the Ashburton Mining Company and the Hercules dredge.
  • U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, Enhancing Salmon and Steelhead Habitat—One Truckload at a Time.
  • California environmental/cultural resources documentation concerning Nisenan occupation and early mining along the American River.

title: Chinese Diggings Across from Sailor Bar
excerpt: A Gold Rush Legacy Visible from Sailor Bar Look across the American River from Sailor Bar toward the steep bluff on the opposite bank. Among the trees and vegetation, you can…
contentHtml:
A Gold Rush Legacy Visible from Sailor Bar

Look across the American River from Sailor Bar toward the steep bluff on the opposite bank. Among the trees and vegetation, you can see a series of narrow cuts and deep, vertical openings in the face of the bluff.

These unusual features are remnants of the historic mining landscape along the American River. They are commonly associated with the Chinese Diggings, where Chinese miners worked the river’s gold-bearing deposits during the Gold Rush era and the decades that followed.

What Are We Seeing?

The narrow cuts visible in the bluff are the most distinctive surviving evidence of the old workings. They penetrate the steep riverbank in places, exposing layers of gravel and earth.

Gold was deposited in the gravel beds of the American River over thousands of years. During the Gold Rush, miners learned to excavate these deposits and wash the gravel to recover the heavier gold.

As the richest and easiest deposits were worked out, miners returned to ground that had already been mined, searching for gold that remained in the gravel. Mining along the riverbanks could involve cutting into the bluffs and terraces, sometimes producing the narrow excavations that can still be seen today.

The precise history of each individual cut is difficult to establish from the surviving landscape. However, the features are part of a larger area of historic placer mining that was worked by Chinese miners and others during the Gold Rush period.

 

Chinese Miners on the American River

Chinese immigrants played an important role in the mining history of the American River.

Thousands of Chinese immigrants came to California during and after the Gold Rush, many from southern China. Chinese miners developed a reputation for patiently reworking older mining areas, recovering gold that remained after earlier operations had removed the richest deposits.

Historical records specifically document Chinese miners working at Sailor Bar and along the American River during the 1850s and 1860s. Their presence was part of a much larger Chinese mining community that developed throughout the Sacramento region.

Their work was often carried out under difficult circumstances. Chinese miners faced widespread discrimination and were frequently pushed onto less desirable claims. Despite these obstacles, they continued to make an important contribution to California’s mining economy.

Reading the Landscape

The Chinese Diggings are a reminder that the Gold Rush was not simply a story of prospectors arriving, finding gold, and moving on.

Mining continued for decades as successive generations of miners searched for gold left behind by earlier operations. The landscape was repeatedly excavated, washed and reshaped.

From Sailor Bar, we can see only a small portion of this historic landscape. Vegetation and erosion have obscured much of the evidence, while the river itself has continued to reshape the bank.

Yet the narrow cuts in the bluff remain visible across the river, providing an intriguing glimpse into the intensive mining that once took place here.

Look Across the River

The next time you visit Sailor Bar, look across the American River at the bluff.

The narrow openings in the bank are easy to overlook. They may appear at first to be simply unusual features of the eroded hillside. But they are part of a landscape shaped by generations of people searching for gold.

These remnants connect us to the Chinese miners and others who worked along the American River more than 150 years ago.

Please observe the historic landscape from a distance. Do not climb, dig into, or remove material from the old workings. What remains is a fragile part of the history of the American River.

title: Gold Dredging along the Lower American River
excerpt: By the late 1800s and early 1900s, easily accessible gold had largely been depleted. Mining companies turned to a new method: gold dredging , which dramatically reshaped areas…
contentHtml:
By the late 1800s and early 1900s, easily accessible gold had largely been depleted. Mining companies turned to a new method: gold dredging, which dramatically reshaped areas like Sailor Bar.

The Companies Behind Sailor Bar’s Dredging and Gravel-Mining History

Today, Sailor Bar is known for its trails, wildlife, fishing, boating, birdwatching and beautiful stretches of the American River. But the landscape visitors see today was shaped in large measure by a very different era—when Sailor Bar was one of the important gold-dredging sites along the American River.

Beginning around the turn of the twentieth century, large floating dredges systematically excavated the gravel deposits at Sailor Bar in search of gold. The machines dug deep into the river terrace and floodplain, processed enormous quantities of gravel, and then deposited the unwanted rock behind them. The long, irregular piles of rounded cobbles and gravel that characterize portions of Sailor Bar today are the surviving dredge tailings from this era.

The Ashburton Mining Company

The most important company in Sailor Bar’s dredging history was the Ashburton Mining Company of Boston.

In the spring of 1899, Ashburton sent two test drills to Sailor Bar to determine whether the gravel deposits contained enough gold to justify large-scale dredging. The tests proved promising, and the company leased approximately 310 acres of auriferous gravel land at Sailor Bar and proceeded to construct a large bucket-line dredge. Contemporary accounts describe the property as being on the north side of the American River near Fair Oaks.

Construction of Ashburton’s first dredge began in 1899. The boat was launched in June 1900 and was christened Hercules. Its bucket line consisted of dozens of heavy buckets that continuously scooped gravel from the bottom of the dredge pond. The material was brought aboard, screened and processed to recover gold, while the waste rock was returned to the ground as tailings.

The scale of the operation was extraordinary for its time. A contemporary mining account reported that the Ashburton dredge was capable of handling approximately 3,000 cubic yards of material per day and represented an investment of roughly $100,000—a tremendous sum in the early 1900s.

Ashburton’s No. 1 dredge was eventually rebuilt and improved. According to a 1914 engineering account, the reconstructed dredge was equipped with a new bucket line, new spuds and a belt conveyor for stacking the tailings. The company subsequently built a second dredge, Ashburton No. 2.

The first dredge operated at Sailor Bar from March 1900 through December 1907. The Ashburton Mining Company then continued its dredging operations elsewhere in the American River district, completing its remaining territory near Folsom at the end of 1913.

A California historical study likewise identifies Sailor Bar as having been dredge-mined by the Ashburton Mining Company between approximately 1899 and 1913, and notes that the company’s first dredge was the second bucket-type dredge to operate in the Folsom Mining District. That dredge was destroyed by fire in 1903 and subsequently rebuilt.

A Remarkable Industrial Operation

The technology used at Sailor Bar was impressive.

A bucket-line dredge was essentially a floating mining factory. A continuous chain of large buckets descended from the front of the dredge into the gravel, scooped up material and carried it aboard. There, screens and sluices separated the gold-bearing material from the enormous quantities of rock and gravel.

An account published in 1905 provides an extraordinary description of Ashburton’s operation at Sailor Bar. The dredge initially deposited the larger boulders directly beneath the barge while finer material was carried through a long swinging sluice. This arrangement allowed the discarded material to be redistributed across the mined area.

Sailor_Bar_Gold_Dredge_Article

The operation was powered by electricity supplied from the Folsom area. Contemporary descriptions indicate that the dredge employed several electric motors, including a 500-horsepower motor to operate the bucket line.

In other words, what may look today like a collection of natural gravel hills and rocky terraces is, in many places, an industrial landscape created by machinery more than a century ago.

Other Companies in the American River Gold-Dredging District

Sailor Bar was part of a much larger gold-dredging industry that developed along the American River between Folsom and the Sacramento area.

The Colorado Pacific Gold Dredging Company, for example, began dredging in the American River district in 1899 at Mississippi Bar, downstream from Sailor Bar. Its dredges were among the early large-scale bucket dredges in the region.

Other companies active in the broader Folsom/American River district included the Folsom Development Company, El Dorado Gold Dredging Company, and Natomas Development Company. By the early 1900s, these operations had helped transform the American River corridor into one of California’s major gold-dredging districts.

The later Natomas Consolidated of California became particularly important in the American River mining industry. Historical records indicate that by 1909 the company controlled more than 5,600 acres of dredgeable land in Sacramento County and operated numerous dredges in the American River district. However, it is important not to confuse these larger regional operations with the specific dredging history of Sailor Bar: the strongest historical documentation identifies Ashburton Mining Company as the company that actually dredged Sailor Bar during its principal early dredging period.

From Gold Mining to Gravel

Gold was not the only legacy of these operations.

The dredges moved enormous quantities of river gravel in their search for gold. What remained was deposited as dredger tailings—the distinctive piles of rounded cobbles and gravel that still cover portions of Sailor Bar.

Sacramento County records describe Sailor Bar as the site of extensive gold-dredging operations from approximately 1900 to 1962, although the historical sources indicate that the major Ashburton dredging era occurred much earlier. The later period reflects the continuation of mining activity in the broader area. The dredging dramatically altered the original landscape, leaving behind largely unvegetated tailing piles and creating the unusual topography visible at Sailor Bar today.

Commercial sand and gravel production along the Lower American River  

The history of Sailor Bar did not end with the gold dredges.  Sand and gravel production continued on both the south shore and the north shore of the river.  One of the largest aggregate operations in the Central Valley took place in the area that is now known as Gold River.   The coarse dredge tailings that remained after the dredging ceased were washed, crushed and graded. This plant was leased to Coast Rock and Gravel Company in 1920 and became part of Pacific Coast Aggregates in 1929.   In the 50’s and 60s huge rock crushers operated 24 hours a day and the sound of the crushers could be heard all over Fair Oaks.   In addition, the Fair Oaks Gravel Company processed and sold sand, gravel, rock and ready mix concrete  at Sailor Bar as well.   

 

Over time, nature began to reclaim this industrial landscape. Trees and other vegetation took root in the sheltered ravines between the tailings. Today, those same areas provide valuable habitat for birds and other wildlife.

What Is a Gold Dredge?

 

A gold dredge was essentially a floating industrial mining machine — part boat, part factory. They operated in large ponds they created as they dug. Some dredges were the size of multi-story buildings and ran continuously, often 24 hours a day.

 

How Dredges Worked (Step-by-Step)

1. Digging with the Bucket Line — A continuous chain of large steel buckets rotated at the front of the dredge, scooping up gravel, sand, and sediment from the riverbed, including ancient river deposits buried deep underground.
2. Lifting Material — Buckets carried material up into the dredge and dumped it into processing equipment onboard.
3. Processing for Gold — Material passed through screens and crushers. Water was used to wash and separate sediment. Gold, being heavier, settled into sluices or riffles.
4. Discarding Tailings — Waste rock and gravel were dumped out the back, creating long rows of rock piles called tailings.
5. Self-Advancing Operation — As the dredge dug forward, it floated in its own pond. The pond moved with the dredge as it advanced across the landscape.

 

What Makes Sailor Bar Unique

 

The rock piles (tailings) seen today at Sailor Bar are direct evidence of dredging. These piles often appear as long ridges or windrows and unnaturally uniform rock fields. The original landscape — soil, vegetation, and river channels — was completely reworked.

Scale and Impact

 

Dredges could process thousands of cubic yards of material per day. Entire sections of the American River floodplain were transformed. Natural habitats were destroyed and replaced with rocky, barren terrain.

Dredging required large crews and constant maintenance. Machinery wear and breakdowns were common. Operations depended on water availability and stable economic conditions.

Environmental Legacy

 

  • Loss of native vegetation and soil structure
  • Altered river channels and floodplain dynamics
  • Long-term habitat disruption

Today, some areas have been naturally or intentionally restored, but the dredger impact is still clearly visible.

contentHtml:
According to local legend, Sailor Bar was named for sailors who abandoned their ship during the Gold Rush to seek their fortune along the American River.

Early prospectors planned for gold by hand and later used cradles, rockers and long-toms Remnants of what have been historically been called, “Chinese Diggings” can still be seen today cut into the Bluffs at Sailor Bar.

These formations appear as narrow trenches. During the 1890s and early 1900s water was used to hydraulically separate gold from the sand and gravel. Later large bucket-line dredges would be used along the river’s flood plain to mine for gold. The massive machines would dig deep into the flood plain of the river, churning up river sediments, and leaving behind the distinctive piles of rounded rock tailings still visible throughout the park today. 

Estimated value of gold recovered by the dredges in the Folsom area alone, was at least $125 million in gold. In today’s dollars, that equals $15 billion.

title: How the American River has Changed over Time
excerpt: The current channel of the lower American River is narrower, deeper, and artificially constrained by levees and dams compared to its channel prior to the Gold Rush. Prior to…
contentHtml:
The current channel of the lower American River is narrower, deeper, and artificially constrained by levees and dams compared to its channel prior to the Gold Rush.  Prior to the Gold Rush, the American River frequently changed its course across the valley floor and once flowed through sections of present-day East Sacramento before being artificially redirected toward Sutter’s Landing. 

During and immediately after the Gold Rush, the bed of the lower American River rose drastically due to a massive influx of mining debris.

Bed Elevation Rise:

In 1879, sediment storage calculations estimated that the lower American River’s channel bed was 5 to 30 feet (1.5 to 9 meters) higher than its pre-Gold Rush state.

The Cause:

This extreme rise, known as channel aggradation (bed raising), was fueled by hydraulic mining. During the Gold Rush era, hydraulic mining dumped massive volumes of  gravel, sand, mud and cobble from the Sierra Nevada mountains  directly into the river system.  

Impact on the American River:

Because the riverbed filled with debris, the river channel lost its capacity to hold water. Normal winter flows suddenly caused catastrophic flooding. To protect the city from the rising water levels, the City of Sacramento undertook a massive engineering project in the 1860s and 1870s to raise its streets and buildings by up to 9.5 feet.

Following the outlawing of unrestricted hydraulic mining and the later construction of Folsom Dam, the river spent the 20th century cutting back down through this historical sediment. Today, the channel has largely eroded back down near its original, pre-Gold Rush baseline.

The American River Channel Today

The completion of Folsom Dam in 1955 as well as other flood control improvements once again has completely changed the dynamics of the American River. In addition, the modern river is now bound tightly by constructed flood control levees along much of its 30-mile urban stretch. Historically, seasonal high waters regularly overtopped natural banks, spreading across wide floodplains and low-lying basins.

Bed Incision and Sediment:

Following the construction of Folsom Dam and Nimbus Dam in the 1950s, sediment was trapped behind the barriers. Deprived of a natural supply of new gravel and sand from upstream, the modern river has actively eroded and lowered its own bed (incision) over the decades.

Fixed Alignment vs. Migration:

Historically, the river frequently changed its course across the valley floor and once flowed through sections of present-day East Sacramento before being artificially redirected toward Sutter’s Landing. Today, bank protection projects and levees lock the channel in place.

The Impact of Folsom and Nimbus Dam

Because Folsom Dam and Nimbus Dam completely block the natural flow of gravel, sand, and cobble from the Sierra Nevada mountains, the lower American River is now locked in a long-term sediment deficit.

As the river flows downstream, it retains its energy but has no incoming debris to carry. This creates “hungry water” that actively erodes the river’s own bed and banks. Over time, this dynamic will trigger several permanent changes to the future channel:

1. Continued Channel Incision (Bed Lowering)

Without a fresh supply of upstream gravel to replenish the riverbed, high-flow events will continue to scour and erode the channel bottom. Historical studies have tracked the riverbed lowering at rates up to 8.2 cm per year in some areas. In the future, the channel will continue to dig itself deeper into the valley floor, further disconnecting the river from what remains of its natural floodplain. 

2. Armoring of the Riverbed

As the river scours the bed, it easily washes away finer materials like sand and small pebbles. Over time, only the largest, heaviest rocks and boulders are left behind. This process is called channel armoring. Eventually, the riverbed will become so heavily armored with coarse rock that the water will no longer be able to erode downward, effectively locking the channel depth in place but leaving a harsh, rocky floor. 

3. Accelerated Lateral Erosion and Bank Failures

When a riverbed becomes heavily armored and cannot erode downward any further, the water’s energy shifts sideways. The future channel will experience increased lateral erosion, aggressively biting into its banks. Because much of the lower river is bordered by urban areas, this creates a perpetual battle for flood managers. Agencies like the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers must continuously install artificial bank protection—like rock rip-rap and deep seepage walls—to stop the river from washing away the levees. 

4. Loss of Salmon Spawning Habitat

The sediment deficit has severe consequences for native wildlife. Chinook salmon and steelhead trout require loose, golf-ball-sized river gravel to build their nests (redds). As the existing gravel washes downstream into the Sacramento River and no new gravel replaces it, the spawning habitat naturally depletes.

Human Intervention: The Artificial Fix

To counteract this grim outlook, the future of the lower American River will rely on heavy human management: 

Gravel Augmentation:

Local environmental coalitions like the Water Forum routinely dump thousands of tons of clean, sorted gravel directly into the river below Nimbus Dam. This gives salmon a place to spawn and gives the “hungry water” something to carry, intentionally slowing down the erosion of the natural channel.

title: Native American History
excerpt: bedrock mortars on the shoreline of Sailor Bar The Nisenan People For thousands of years, the lower American River was home to the Nisenan people — village-based communities…
contentHtml:
The Nisenan People

For thousands of years, the lower American River was home to the Nisenan people — village-based communities whose lives were woven into the rhythms of the river. They practiced seasonal movement tied to natural cycles and possessed deep ecological knowledge and stewardship of the land. The river was central to life — providing food, materials, and cultural identity.

Daily Life

Staple foods included acorns, salmon, deer, seeds, and berries. The Nisenan crafted tools from stone, bone, and plant fibers, and maintained extensive trade networks with neighboring peoples.

One of the most important cultural features at Sailor Bar is the presence of bedrock mortars — small, rounded depressions ground into flat rock surfaces. These features can still be found in parts of the American River Parkway and are powerful evidence of long-term Nisenan presence.

What Are Bedrock Mortars?

  • Bowl-shaped holes worn into granite or other hard rock
  • Created over generations by repeated grinding
  • Often found in clusters, indicating communal food preparation areas

How They Were Used

The Nisenan relied heavily on acorns, which require careful processing to make them edible.

Step-by-Step Acorn Processing

  1. Gathering — Acorns were collected from oak trees in the fall. Different oak species provided slightly different flavors and qualities.
  2. Drying and Storage — Acorns were dried and stored for year-round use.
  3. Shelling — Outer shells were removed by hand.
  4. Grinding in Bedrock Mortars — Acorns were placed into the mortar holes. A pestle (a hand-held stone tool) was used to pound and grind them into meal. Repeated use over centuries deepened the mortar holes.
  5. Leaching (Critical Step) — Ground acorn meal contains tannins, which are bitter and toxic. Meal was placed in sand basins or baskets, and water was poured over it repeatedly to remove the tannins.
  6. Cooking — The resulting flour was cooked into mush, soup, or bread-like foods.

Cultural Importance

  • Acorns were a dietary staple, providing reliable nutrition
  • Grinding was often a communal and social activity
  • Mortar sites were gathering places, often used for generations

What Visitors Should Understand

  • Bedrock mortars can represent hundreds of years of continuous use
  • They are cultural resources and should never be touched or disturbed
  • They connect directly to living descendants of the Nisenan people

Salmon was a Vital Food Source

The Nisenan people relied on salmon as a vital, staple food source and cultural cornerstone, harvesting them from the river using weirs, nets, and harpoons. Salmon was a major seasonal food source that was dried, smoked, or pounded into flour for storage, allowing the Nisenan to maintain food security throughout the year.

Along with acorns, salmon was one of the most important foods for the Nisenan, who established permanent villages near salmon-producing rivers and honored them through traditions. The Nisenan treated salmon with profound respect, viewing the returning fish as a gift that demanded sustainable practices and ceremonial honor.

Impacts of the Gold Rush on the Nisenan People

 

Displacement and Loss of Land

 

The arrival of miners during the Gold Rush had devastating consequences for the Nisenan people. Thousands of miners flooded into the American River region beginning in 1848. Traditional Nisenan lands along the river were quickly occupied, mined, and settled. Villages were destroyed or abandoned as access to land and resources was lost.

Destruction of Food Sources

 

Mining operations severely disrupted the natural environment:

  • Salmon runs declined due to water diversion, sediment, and habitat destruction
  • Oak woodlands and plant resources were damaged or cleared
  • Game animals were overhunted or driven away

This led to widespread food scarcity and starvation among the Nisenan.

Violence and Disease

Many Native people faced violence from miners and settlers. There were documented massacres and forced removals throughout Northern California. Introduced diseases (such as smallpox and measles) spread rapidly, as Native populations had no immunity. The population of Native Californians declined dramatically during this period.

Loss of Culture and Lifeways

 

Traditional seasonal movement and cultural practices were disrupted. Sacred sites and village locations were destroyed or made inaccessible. Many Nisenan people were forced into labor or relocated to missions and ranches.

Resilience and Continuity

 

Despite these hardships, the Nisenan people endured:

  • Descendants of the Nisenan still live in the region today
  • Cultural traditions, ecological knowledge, and connections to the land continue
  • There are ongoing efforts to revitalize language, culture, and land stewardship practices

title: Remembering Camp Sabadaca
excerpt: Camp Sabadaca is the name for the Sailor Bar Day Camp which was operated at Sailor Bar in the 1980’s by the Fair Oaks Recreation and Park District (FORPD). Camp Sabadaca…
contentHtml:
Camp Sabadaca is the name for the Sailor Bar Day Camp which was operated at Sailor Bar in the 1980’s by the Fair Oaks Recreation and Park District (FORPD).    Camp Sabadaca emphasized nature and outdoor activities, catering to children and families in the Fair Oaks area.

The name “Camp Sabadaca” is derived from the first two letters of each word in “Sailor Bar Day Camp”.   The camp offered a variety of engaging activites for youths aged 7 to 12, including overnight camping, crafts, hiking, games, and field trips.

Participants participated in two weeks of overnight camping experiences and engaged in various craft activities to encourage creativity and skill development.   Outdoor hiking was also a key component of the program which promoted physical fitness and exploration.   Kids also participated in games to encourage teamwork and fun.  Finally, campers also enjoyed field trips to enhance their learning and adventure.

The kids who participated in Camp Sabadaca back in the 80’s are now adults in their forties.  They have nothing but extreme praise for their experiences at the camp.  Their feeling is that Camp Sabadaca at Sailor Bar with its woodlands and river engendered in the kids who participated a genuine feeling of being part of the land – a true connection to it and the desire to preserve its wild nature.  The participants  gained a sense of responsibility and stewardship.  Because they treasured being in the surroundings, they were extra careful to ‘stay on the deer paths and never litter’.  Each day they all participated in songs, nature activities and scavenger hunts all over Sailor Bar, collecting raw materials to fashion into ‘earthy crafts’.

These participants (who are now adults) express that it was wonderful for the kids that the FORPD hired high school and college students to lead the hikes, nature art projects, singing, etc.  Of course, having the older students truly seemed so cool to the camp kids!

title: The Ghost of Sailor Bar
excerpt: Sailor Bar is noted for its historic native American grinding rocks on its shoreline as well as for its gold mining history. The park is named for sailors who allegedly jumped…
contentHtml:
Sailor Bar is noted for its historic native American grinding rocks on its shoreline as well as for its gold mining history.   The park is named for sailors who allegedly jumped ship during the gold rush to mine for gold.   Several huge gold dredges operated at Sailor Bar in the early 1900’s, leaving huge rock piles throughout the park. 
 
In 1908 a newspaper article was published which talked about a “Ghost of Sailor Bar” .  This story was republished by the San Juan Record on September 28th,  1977.   (The San Juan Record was published from 1933-1980).  More recently mysterious rock cairns have appeared throughout the park and some people are wondering if the Ghost of Sailor Bar could could still be present at Sailor Bar!

title: Aerojet Groundwater Pumps
excerpt: Protecting the American River: The Aerojet Groundwater Pumping Systems at Sailor Bar Beneath the peaceful trails and riverbanks of Sailor Bar Park in Fair Oaks lies a vital,…
contentHtml:
Protecting the American River: The Aerojet Groundwater Pumping Systems at Sailor Bar
Beneath the peaceful trails and riverbanks of Sailor Bar Park in Fair Oaks lies a vital, hidden environmental safeguarding effort: the Sailor Bar groundwater extraction and treatment infrastructure operated by Aerojet Rocketdyne. While visitors come to Sailor Bar to hike, raft, and fish, parts of the park play an active role in the multi-decade cleanup of the neighboring Aerojet Superfund Site.
The History and Purpose of the Extraction Wells
Decades of aerospace research, rocket testing, and chemical manufacturing at Aerojet’s sprawling Rancho Cordova facility—located south of the American River—led to historical soil and groundwater contamination, specifically involving volatile organic compounds (VOCs). To prevent underground contaminant plumes from migrating, expanding, or reaching the American River, regulatory agencies including the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board mandated an extensive network of pump-and-treat systems.
Specific groundwater extraction wells are located directly within Sailor Bar Park to intercept the leading edge of these underground plumes north of the river.
How the System Works
  • Extraction: Hidden wells safely pump contaminated groundwater from deep beneath the Sailor Bar area.
  • Conveyance: The extracted water is piped across or away from the park to dedicated treatment plants, such as the Aerojet Groundwater Extraction Treatment (ARGET) facility located south of the river.
  • Purification and Discharge: The water undergoes rigorous treatment to remove impurities and regularly meets strict standards set by the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) before it is safely returned to local waterways.

Coexisting with Nature and Recreation
The pumping infrastructure at Sailor Bar is largely unobtrusive, designed to blend into the surrounding landscape so that park visitors can enjoy the recreation areas without interruption. Oversight by state and federal environmental agencies ensures that the extraction operations continue safely, effectively shielding the lower American River ecosystem and regional drinking water supplies from historical industrial impacts.

title: Great Horned Owl Nest East of Sailor Bar
excerpt: A hidden nest with a remarkable view The steep bluffs above the river just to the east of the Sailor Bar Boat Launch are home to a remarkable sight—a nesting cavity used by a…
contentHtml:
A hidden nest with a remarkable view

The steep bluffs above the river just to the east of the Sailor Bar Boat Launch are home to a remarkable sight—a nesting cavity used by a Great Horned Owl.

The nest is difficult to see from Sailor Bar itself. The best opportunity to observe it is from the opposite side of the river, near the Nimbus Fish Hatchery, where the bluff can be viewed from a different angle.

It is a fitting reminder that the American River Parkway is more than a place for people to hike, fish, and enjoy the river. The cliffs, trees, shrubs, and riparian forests along the river provide shelter and nesting habitat for an extraordinary variety of wildlife.

A very unusual nest site

Great Horned Owls are remarkably adaptable when it comes to choosing a nest. Unlike many birds, they do not normally construct their own nests. Instead, they often take over an abandoned nest built by another large bird, such as a hawk, crow, raven, heron, or eagle.

But they are not limited to tree nests. Great Horned Owls may also nest in natural cavities, caves, on cliff ledges, and in other sheltered locations.

The Sailor Bar owl appears to have taken advantage of exactly this kind of habitat—a protected cavity in the steep river bluff.

The Sacramento Audubon Society has documented Great Horned Owls using riverbank cavities in this area. In February 2026, an Audubon field trip at the Nimbus Fish Hatchery reported seeing a Great Horned Owl occupying a “riverbank cave nest.”

 

A predator perfectly suited to the river corridor

Great Horned Owls are among the largest and most powerful owls in North America. Their distinctive feather tufts give them their familiar “horned” appearance, although those tufts are not actually ears.

They are primarily nocturnal hunters. From a high perch, an owl can listen and watch for prey before silently swooping down to capture it. Their diet is remarkably varied and can include rats, mice, rabbits, squirrels, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and other animals.

The American River corridor provides an excellent combination of habitats for a hunting owl: dense riparian vegetation for cover and roosting, open areas where prey can be detected, and the river bluffs themselves for protected nesting and resting places.

Great Horned Owls are also remarkably adaptable. They can live in forests, river valleys, grasslands, agricultural areas, parks, and even urban environments.

Look—but give the owl some space

A nest like this is exciting to discover, but it is important to remember that the owl’s home is not a viewing attraction. During nesting season, disturbance can cause unnecessary stress to the adults and young.

Fortunately, this nest can be appreciated from across the river. Please do not attempt to approach the cavity, climb the bluff, or enter the area around the nest. Binoculars or a spotting scope provide a much better—and safer—way to observe the birds.

Audubon recommends keeping a good distance from nesting owls and avoiding playback of owl calls, particularly during breeding season. Shining lights at owls should also be avoided.

An unexpected neighbor at Sailor Bar

The Great Horned Owl is one of many species that share the American River corridor with the people who visit Sailor Bar.

From the park, visitors may notice hawks circling overhead, herons along the river, songbirds moving through the willows and cottonwoods, and occasionally the unmistakable silhouette of a large owl.

The owl nest across the river is a particularly special discovery because it is almost invisible from the park. It illustrates an important lesson about the American River Parkway:

Wildlife habitat doesn’t always announce itself. Sometimes you have to stop, look across the river, and know where to look.

Where can you see the nest?

The nesting cavity is located in the steep bluff along the American River just east of Sailor Bar. It is not readily visible from Sailor Bar. The best viewing opportunity is from the vicinity of the Nimbus Fish Hatchery, looking across the river toward the bluff.

If you are fortunate enough to spot the owl, enjoy the sight from a distance and allow this remarkable resident of the American River to remain undisturbed.

Did you know?

Great Horned Owls don’t usually build their own nests.

They commonly reuse abandoned nests built by other large birds, but they can also nest in cavities, caves, cliffs, and ledges. Their willingness to use such a wide variety of nest sites is one reason they are able to thrive in so many different environments.

title: Grinding Rocks
excerpt: The historic bedrock grinding rocks along the shoreline of Sailor Bar Park in Fair Oaks provide a tangible, silent connection to the Nisenan people who inhabited the lower…
contentHtml:
The historic bedrock grinding rocks along the shoreline of Sailor Bar Park in Fair Oaks provide a tangible, silent connection to the Nisenan people who inhabited the lower American River canyons long before the Gold Rush. 
 

Embedded into the exposed hardpan and river rocks, these smooth, bowl-shaped depressions—often called bedrock mortars or milling slicks—were used over generations by Indigenous women to process and grind staple foods like wild acorns, seeds, and nuts. Unlike the surrounding landscape that was heavily altered by hydraulic mining and bucket-line gold dredges, these ancient stone workspaces remain as a profound cultural landmark. Visitors walking the quiet dirt trails near the water’s edge can spot these historical artifacts, offering a moment to reflect on the deep human history of the American River Parkway.

title: Heron Rookeries
